title: Why TypeScript matters on a public site
excerpt: TypeScript for websites is protection for the next person in the repo. It catches broken props and unsafe edits. It is not a badge to put in the footer.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it. The editor fits a piece about catching a bad edit before the public sees it.
caption: The check happens in the editor, before the page is public. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Why use TypeScript on a marketing site?
faqs.answer: Because the next edit should fail in the editor when a required field is missing, not in the browser when a stranger opens the page. A company site is a set of components with props, and types name those props. They do not make the design better by themselves. They make a careless change louder, sooner.

faqs.question: Does TypeScript make a site faster?
faqs.answer: No. Speed is a property of what you ship to the browser: images, fonts, scripts, and how soon the page can paint. Types are erased before that, so a typed site can still be slow and an untyped site can be quick. Ask for both, and do not let one stand in for the other.

faqs.question: What should a founder be able to see?
faqs.answer: That the repository type-checks in the same place it builds, and that a broken check stops the deploy. You do not have to read the types. You should hear, in the handoff, that the next developer can change a headline component without guessing which fields are required.

markdown:
TypeScript for websites earns its place as protection for the next person in the repository. It catches a missing prop, a mistyped field, and an edit that would have rendered a blank section. It is not a badge for the footer, and it is not a sign that the design is good. A public page can be fully typed and still say nothing useful. The type checker only answers a narrower question: did this change still fit the shapes the page expects?

That narrower question matters because the site will be edited by people who were not in the room when it was written. A founder, a new hire, a different studio. They will touch a component under time pressure. Types are how the codebase refuses a broken edit before a stranger sees it.

## What actually breaks on a company site

A marketing page looks simple and is full of small contracts. A hero expects a headline, a supporting line, and an action. A project card expects a name, a summary, and an image with alt text. A form expects a destination for the message. When those contracts live only in someone's memory, the next edit guesses. The guess is often almost right. Almost right is a page that renders, and then fails in one browser, or omits the button, or ships an image with no description.

JavaScript will let the guess through. The page loads. A value is undefined. A section collapses, or the word undefined appears where a sentence should have been. You find out from a customer, or you do not find out at all. TypeScript moves that failure to the moment of the edit. The field is required. The editor says so. The deploy does not proceed until the shape is honest again.

Google's guidance on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) includes a blunt quality question: is the content produced well, or does it look sloppy or hastily produced? A broken section is that sloppiness, visible to a visitor who does not care what language you used. Types are one way a small team keeps ordinary edits from becoming a hasty public page. They are not a substitute for reading the page.

## Fewer broken props

Think of a prop as a labeled slot. The card component has a slot for the title and a slot for the link. If a new page uses the card and forgets the link, a typed component fails the build. An untyped one invents a clickable area that goes nowhere, or throws when someone clicks.

The same protection applies to content that comes from a CMS. The type describes what a post is allowed to be: a title, a slug, a date, a body. When the CMS shape changes, the type either updates with it or the build fails. That failure is a gift. The silent alternative is a template that assumes a field exists and renders a hole where the field used to be.

Hanabi writes the public site in TypeScript, with React. The habit is ordinary. Components say what they require. Shared content types say what a page is. A review looks for a cast that silences the checker, because a silenced checker is a rumor that the code is fine. The point is not to collect types. The point is that the next person can change a section and learn immediately whether they kept the contract.

## Safer edits, not a ceremony

A useful type is close to the language the team already uses. Headline is a string. Image has a source and an alt string. The action has a label and a URL. You do not need a thicket of generic helpers to get the benefit on a marketing site. If the types are harder to read than the component, people will work around them, and the protection disappears.

Run the check where the work already happens. Locally, before a commit, and again in the deploy. A check that only one developer remembers to run is a suggestion. A check that blocks a broken build is a policy. Founders do not need to operate the checker. They need to know it is not optional.

Leave room for content that is genuinely flexible. A rich text body is not a fixed list of fields, and pretending it is will fight the editor. Type the envelope: this page has a title and a body. Do not try to type every possible sentence. The safety you want is against structural mistakes, not against prose.

## What types will not do

They will not make the site fast. The checker runs before the browser. Images, fonts, and third-party scripts still decide whether the page appears quickly. A team can hide inside the type system and ship a heavy page. Ask for speed as its own requirement.

They will not make the sentence true. A typed headline can still be vague. They will not choose the brand, the structure, or the offer. They will not stop a person from publishing a page that is polished and empty. Read the site. The checker cannot.

They will not replace a review of the actual page on a phone. A component can satisfy the types and still overflow, still hide the button under a browser bar, still fail contrast. Types are the layer that keeps the data honest. Design review keeps the page honest. You want both, and you should not let either impersonate the other.

## How to ask for it in a handoff

Ask where the types live, in one sentence. The answer should sound like the components and the content, not like a configuration trophy. Ask what happens if a required field is removed. The answer should be that the build fails. Ask who can run the project. The answer should include a person who was not the original author, following the README.

If the answer is that TypeScript is there because serious teams use it, you have the badge and not the protection. Look for a recent component and see whether its props are named in the language of the page. Title, image, action. Those names are the system. The compiler is the guard.

Clean code, on a marketing site, is the wider habit this belongs to. [What clean code means on a marketing site](/blog/clean-code-on-a-marketing-site) is the next piece, about a later editor being able to find the headline, the sections, and the images without a treasure hunt.

When you want a public site built so the next edit is safe, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). TypeScript is part of that care. It is not the care by itself.
